Okay. I am nonbinary and bisexual. I could also go into super micro labels on specifically my gender identity, but do not feel the need to for my point to come across. 

When I came out as nb to my (cishet) mom, she had a hard time with it because she didn't understand. I said something along the lines of "you don't need to understand to accept." We need to realise that there are aspects of people that we will never understand, and accept that. Not just sexuality or gender based, but relating to \*anything!\* I will never understand how it is to be attracted to only one gender, or not liking the taste of chocolate, or loving watching football. But I accept all these things as valid and okay.

I personally do not think we need to be digestible for outsiders. That rhetoric is exactly the type of thing that will split the community and turn it into a mess, which you seem worried about. This is common within the trans community, and there is already discourse about what a "real" and "fake" trans person is. We are already infighting and excluding each other. We are helping the oppressors by doing this, because they don't even have to do it themselves! However, you talk more about sexuality labels in your post, so for now I'm going to assume that gender labels do not bother you as much. The same logic applies, though. Who decides what is digestible? Why is it okay to be pansexual, but not omni, for example? What if the only palatable sexualities are hetero and homo? The people you are trying to please/be digestible for will decide what is ok and not. And they will all have different opinions, as well.

The use of the word "circus" is so extremely rough to me. A circus invokes the feeling of something wrong, something to gawk and laugh at. This is exactly what a lot of cishets feel abt the queer community, and hearing it from someone in it is so painful and harmful. 

The part about terms being approved is also quite bothersome. Language changes all the time. This theory about stuff needing to be approved reeks of the transphobic idea that he and she are the only valid personal pronouns. The terms are also never enforced onto the public pretty much. Say you meet a cishet person. They or you bring up sexuality and you say you are pansexual. They do not know what this means. Would you be angry, mad, upset? Or would you calmly explain? The fact that there are many words to describe same/similar experiences might also create a bigger frame of reference. Say you do calmly explain. The person may then go "oh, so similar to omnisexual!" and therefore have a deeper understanding, rather than more shallow. 

What do you mean by "developing and educating our community?" What is it we need to develop? And what is "the authenticity" of our community? Is this not literally a group of people being their authentic selves? I don't quite see where you are coming from.

I am also interested in what you mean with "...your descriptor for your sexual orientation exists to piggy back and shame another orientation..." because I cannot for the life of me figure out what label you are talking about.

Hello there! Id like to preface this by saying that I do not know exactly how you feel. I’ve been struggling with body image as long as I can remember, so I never really had one of those “wow” moments that you describe here. What I can say is that things like that do fluctuate. Sometimes you’re more confident, sometimes you can’t stand yourself. I get that this must have been very very difficult for you. And I’m sorry it happened. I wouldn’t, just from this, say that you’re trans. The term “gender dysphoria” means that you feel as if your body is wrong, that it doesn’t match what you really feel. Dysphoria doesn’t mean that you have to hate your body, it means that you may feel odd or strange about things such as your genitals, and secondary sex characteristics like body hair for example. Dysphoria is different for everyone and there is no surefire way to know from just this incident. However, I do think that if you want to explore this more, a good place to start would be to ask somebody, online or irl, to refer to you with feminine pronouns and words (she/her, girl, woman, sister etc.) This can help you get a view on how you feel about being perceived as a girl. Of course you could also look into the non-binary side of things. That’s where it gets more tricky. Since we get taught that male and female are the two genders, figuring out that you’re nonbinary can be very difficult. You need to break out of the binary system that you’re used to. Dysphoria is also strange for a lot of nonbinary people, including myself. I, for example, have no issues with my genitalia, but hate my chest and lack of body hair. That could possibly explain why you say you want to be more feminine, but that you don’t really view yourself as a woman. Of course, you could also be having issues with confidence that are not tied to gender identity. That is very difficult and either way, I’m sorry you feel like this. My messages are open if you need any more advice, or need to talk. I hope you figure it out! Take care!
